1:
What drew Jonathan is the first question, and the answers differ in kind. Henry puts it down to the speaking itself, since David had answered the king with prudence, modesty and piety, in a manner at once bold and sweet, the more surprising in a man of his disadvantages. Ellicott denies that the gallantry or the skill of the combat could account for it, and names the shepherd's childlike trust in the arm of the Lord as the thing that won the prince, who had himself gone up against a garrison with none but his armour-bearer on the same conviction. Henry notices the same parallel and draws from it a near resemblance of affections which made the two seem one soul in two bodies, a phrase Clarke takes from the ancients along with their maxim that a friend is another self.

The present of the robe and the armour is read as courtesy or as custom. Gill and Henry both take it for a deliberate re-clothing: the prince was uneasy to see so great a soul in a shepherd's dress, and put him at a stroke into the habit of a courtier and a soldier, a sword and bow for the staff and sling, a girdle for the scrip. Henry presses the detail that these were the clothes Jonathan was wearing, and that Saul's armour had not fitted David while Jonathan's did, their bodies being of a size as their minds were of a piece. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both set the act beside the exchange of armour between Glaucus and Diomedes, the one adding that the custom reappears among the early Celts, the other quoting the lines on brass given for gold.

The covenant is weighed for what it was worth afterwards. Gill makes it a mutual undertaking to maintain each other's interest in life and after death, whichever of them survived, and traces the result, that David had a friend at court who pleaded his cause, uncovered his father's plots and saved his life. Henry finds it remarkable that men so entirely satisfied with each other at a first meeting should want it bound, and answers that true love desires to be constant and an honest mind does not startle at assurances. Ellicott makes the bond a shared determination to do the will of the God they both believed loved Israel, and follows it to the last meeting of the two in the wilderness, where the elder strengthened the younger's hand in God. Henry's own use of it is to turn the stripping into a figure of Christ, who emptied himself to enrich us and went further, since he put on our rags while Jonathan did not put on David's.

The promotion that followed is described in three different ranks. Clarke makes him generalissimo, what a later age would call field marshal. Keil and Delitzsch say only that he was set above the men of war as one of their commanders. Henry denies the generalship on the ground that Abner held it, and suggests the command of the lifeguard, or precedence given out of turn in recompense for his service. Gill and Wesley fix the moment: the king took him home the same day, and he had not until then lived at court. Ellicott dwells on the power this man had over the hearts of those he was overtaking in the race for honour, so that he disarmed the jealousy such a rise would provoke; Keil and Delitzsch make the same point of the courtiers, who are envious as a rule. Henry's reflection is on David rather than the court, that bearing sudden honour without being lifted up took more grace than bearing hardship, since it is harder to know how to abound than how to be abased. Clarke's one textual note is that the Greek version omits these five verses altogether.
6:
The triumph is dated and then described. Ellicott denies that this is the homecoming after the giant fell, and places it at the close of the campaign that followed, a run of victories which restored Israel's supremacy for a time. Clarke makes celebrating victories the particular business of certain women, and makes their instruments three-stringed, which he would render sistrums, the Egyptian brass frame whose loose rods jingle when shaken. Henry has the king making a triumphal progress through the nearer cities, the song supplied by some poet who admired David's bravery and was more just than wise in giving his achievements the preference. Keil and Delitzsch add that Thenius assigns the section to another source, partly because the javelin scene recurs later.

The arithmetic of the song is read three ways. Clarke holds that it cannot be a count of the slain and makes it the odds faced instead, that Saul had been opposed by thousands and David by ten thousands. Henry answers the grievance on its own ground: the song looked only at the late action, in which the killing of Goliath in effect defeated the whole Philistine army, so that it gave David no more than his due. Ellicott treats the couplet as the refrain of an old national song, quoted again later in the book. Henry's judgement is that a prince should have been above noticing a slight to his personal honour when the public glory was sincerely meant, and that proud men cannot bear to hear anyone praised but themselves. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both quote Gerlach, that a king standing powerless while a shepherd boy decided the victory was shown one more mark of his rejection.

From that day the looking changes, and so does the malady. Gill gives the verb both senses, a sour and envious look and a watching of every motion for treason, the Targum making it a lying in wait. Ellicott describes an alternation, the king longing for the one man who could charm away his melancholy while dreading his influence, with the hate slowly obscuring the old love. His account of the madness is that it changed form, the earlier torpor giving way to a jealousy that drove him to open violence and dark plots by turns. Keil and Delitzsch settle the disputed verb shortly, that here it means to rave, and Ellicott supports this from the conjugation, which is never used of true prophecy. Wesley notices that the fit returned the very next day after the envy was conceived, and calls it the fruit of envy.

Whether the fit was genuine divides the voices. Clarke takes the same conjugation the other way, since it can mean to feign an action, concluding that the king pretended to be at family prayer to conceal his intention and keep David, who was probably supplying the music, unsuspicious. Henry reaches the same conclusion by another road, that the ecstasy was put on to decoy David within reach, with the design of imputing the murder to a divine impulse afterwards. On the javelin the accounts differ: Keil and Delitzsch have it thrown and missing because David turned away twice, while Ellicott prefers the Alexandrian and Chaldee reading, that it was lifted or aimed, and argues that a man who had had it thrown at him would hardly have trusted himself in that chamber again. Clarke explains why the weapon was at hand, since the spear was the emblem of regal authority, and cites Justin for the age when kings carried a spear instead of a diadem and spears were worshipped as images of the gods. Henry's contrast is the one the scene is remembered by, David with his harp seeking to serve and Saul with his javelin seeking to kill; of the escape he says David did as bravely in getting out of the way as in running upon Goliath.
12:
The fear is explained three ways, and none of them is simple cowardice. Gill grounds it in the plain fact the verse gives, that the Lord was with David to protect and prosper him, and reports the Targum's rendering that the word of the Lord was his help and the reading which takes it of the Holy Ghost. His own addition is psychological: in his melancholy fits the king might expect the man he had tried to kill to watch for an opportunity and seize the kingdom. Ellicott makes it the clearest-sighted moment the king has, since he was conscious that his old vigour was deserting him and recognised in David a power that had once been his own. Henry allows that the fear may have been partly a pretence, since men who design ill against others like it thought that others design ill against them, and David's withdrawal was evidence enough against the charge. His conclusion is that the awe was genuine, as Herod's was of John, and that the king knew he had lost the presence of God while David had it.

Why David was sent away is disputed in the same spirit. Clarke calls the command of a thousand a pretence of honour, meant only to rid the court of the object of its envy, and Gill adds the plainer motives, that the king could not bear the sight of him and felt safer at a distance. Wesley gives three reasons together, fear of assassination, the fact that David's presence now made him sadder than the harp had ever made him cheerful, and chiefly a wish to expose him to hazards. Henry agrees on the design and thinks it badly judged, since a command in the country took David away from the courtiers but gave him the people instead. Keil and Delitzsch describe what the post involved, the going out and coming in of a commander whose enterprises prospered so that the blessing of the Lord rested on all he did. Ellicott thinks the darker plan of the next verses may already have been forming while the appointment was being made.

The wisdom the chapter keeps repeating is given its own weight. Gill notes that the word carries prospering as well as behaving wisely, that the conduct held in the camp as in the court, and that David here is a type of Christ. Henry turns the sequence into a maxim: the more wisely David behaved, the more Saul feared him, whereas men who think the way to be feared is to hector and threaten are feared by fools only and despised by the wise and good. His conclusion is that behaving wisely is what makes a man both feared and loved, since wisdom makes the face to shine and commands respect.

The love of the whole nation is read for more than its warmth. Gill observes that the verb is singular, so that every man in the northern tribes loved him as well as his own tribe of Judah. Ellicott takes the naming of Israel and Judah for a sign that the compiler wrote after the separation under Rehoboam, while granting that a marked distinction between north and south existed long before the disruption; his point about David is that a man of Judah was equally popular in the north. Henry's note here runs on into the plots of the following verses, and his judgement on them is the hardest thing said of the king in the chapter. He observes that the conscience which would not let Saul strike at David himself raised no objection to sending him against the Philistines, though the design was as truly murder before God as doing it with his own hand. His other charge is a cheat practised on the world, since the king spoke of a son-in-law while plotting the man's ruin.
17:
The offer of the elder daughter is treated as a debt being paid in bad faith. Ellicott points out that the marriage had been promised long before to whoever killed the Philistine champion, and that the king had put off the performance until a use could be found for it. On his reading the dark thought came while the promise was being honoured, that the hated life might be endangered under cover of keeping faith. Gill says as much in a line, that the words were spoken not in good will but to lay a snare. On the phrase about the Lord's battles Ellicott notes that every patriotic Israelite felt himself warring for the Lord, as David had when he spoke of the giant defying the ranks of the living God, and as the title of a lost collection of songs implies. Clarke adds the qualification he takes from Calmet, that the wars of the Hebrews were truly the Lord's only while they were waged by his express orders, and became wars of lust and profanity once worldly ambition mingled with them.

David's answer is modest, and the modesty turns on a disputed phrase. Gill has him surprised by the offer and not refusing it, but answering with great humility. Keil and Delitzsch agree that he suspected nothing of the craftiness, and render the question as asking what his condition in life and his father's family amounted to; they admit that the words are difficult and that the sense which suggests itself first will not fit the pronoun. Ellicott lists three readings and rejects two: a reference to David's own life, which the opening question has already covered, and the condition of life preferred by Keil, which he doubts the Hebrew word will bear. His own choice follows Ewald and Lange in making it a question about the family, what his relations were that he should be son-in-law to a king. Wesley takes the plainest sense of all, how little his life was worth to be the purchase price of a king's daughter, and finds in the self-abasement a piece of wisdom as well, since it showed the king how far the man was from aspiring to the throne.

The promise was then broken, and the reasons given for it differ. Keil and Delitzsch state the fact without explaining it, that when the time came the daughter was given to a man of whom nothing further is known. Ellicott offers two explanations, a fit of jealousy, or the costly gifts a wealthy suitor could offer for a princess where custom expected them and a comparatively poor man could not compete. He adds what came of the match, five sons who were afterwards hanged before the Lord in the blood revenge the Gibeonites exacted from the king's family, and Wesley, naming the suitor's father, calls the whole transaction an act of great injustice that God accordingly cursed in its children. The omission of these verses by the Greek version is explained differently by the two who notice it: Keil and Delitzsch think the translators dropped them because the first promise came to nothing as far as David was concerned, while Ellicott thinks they could see no reason for the sudden change of purpose.
20:
The younger daughter's love is read as an opportunity the king had been waiting for. Gill accounts for the affection itself by the comeliness of the man, his gallant behaviour and wise conduct, and the general esteem he stood in. Keil and Delitzsch use it to explain the earlier breach of promise, since no pretext is recorded but it appears from the two passages together that the elder daughter had no love for David. Ellicott makes the new offer a fresh excuse to put the man's life in peril while still appearing to honour an old pledge. Gill notes the irony that the woman meant for a snare afterwards became the means of his escape, when messengers were sent to kill him in his own house.

What exactly the snare was to be is explained three ways. Clarke says the condition had already been fixed in the king's mind, a hundred Philistines, which he supposed David would undertake for love of the princess and must necessarily perish in attempting. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the two things the verse states as the king's purpose, that the woman should be a snare and that the hand of the Philistines should be upon him. Ellicott raises a possibility none of the others does, that this plot, which became public knowledge later, is where David found the method he used against Uriah at the siege of Rabbah. On the clause about the second offer Ellicott prefers in this second way to the received rendering, and notes that the Greek version drops the statement because it refers back to the passage it had already omitted.

The courtiers are sent because David had not answered the first approach. Gill explains the manoeuvre, that a man ill used over the elder daughter would not listen to proposals about the younger, so the thing had to be done at second hand, and that the servants delivered their message exactly as ordered. Ellicott passes on Lange's remark that their fluent speech has something of the flattering and conciliatory tone usual in such circles. David's reply turns on his poverty, and the two who weigh it agree on the fact and differ on the feeling. Keil and Delitzsch take the words in perfect sincerity, since a man unable to offer anything like a suitable dowry could not suppose a king would give his daughter without one. Ellicott hears in them a man who reckoned himself a successful soldier of fortune among wealthy chiefs, whose father was head man of a small village and poor beside the elders of the court, and who therefore blamed his earlier disappointment on his own poverty and a richer rival's purse.
24:
The price named in place of a dowry is read for what it reveals of the man who set it. Gill has the servants report the substance of David's answer, his unworthiness and his inability to bring anything suitable, and the king framing his reply to remove that objection in particular. Keil and Delitzsch observe that no dowry was asked at all, only the slaughter of a hundred Philistines with proof that it had been done, ostensibly to avenge the king on his enemies, while the writer states plainly that the design was to have David killed. Clarke explains the proof itself, that the foreskins showed not merely that a hundred men had fallen but that they were of the uncircumcised, and he reports a similar custom still found among the Abyssinians. Ellicott passes on a sharper reading, that the choice of such tokens rather than heads betrays a suspicious and malignant mind: judging others by himself, the king allowed for the possibility that David might kill some of his own Israelite subjects, as he was himself seeking the death of his own deliverer.

That the condition was accepted at all is where the commentators part company. Keil and Delitzsch say simply that David was satisfied, suspecting no craft and loving the woman, and that he did not wait out the time allowed him. Ellicott grants that the king's design succeeded, in the sense that the prospect of the alliance drove the soldier to wilder feats of arms, and then enters the chapter's one moral protest: the ferocity of such a bargain being offered, accepted and overpaid shows what a half-barbarous age this was. Gill reads the same action the opposite way, as evidence of obedience to orders, of sincerity toward the woman for whose sake the risk was run, and of zeal for God and country against their avowed enemies. Ellicott adds the extravagance that Josephus makes the price six hundred heads.

The number itself is a textual question. Gill keeps the two hundred of the Hebrew, stresses that the verb is singular so the deed was David's own, and notes that the Greek version has only one hundred. Clarke argues the other way and prefers the smaller figure, since the bargain was struck for a hundred and David himself afterwards said he had espoused the king's daughter for a hundred. Wesley keeps the doubled number and makes it deliberate, done to bind the king the more firmly to his promise and to show the strength of his affection for the daughter. Keil and Delitzsch end where the plot ends, with the plan for David's certain death failing and the marriage having to be made good.
28:
The chapter closes by naming what the king had been afraid of all along. Gill lists the evidence by which he came to know it, the favour David had among men, the success of everything he undertook, and the way each of the king's own moves had been overruled for David's good; he adds the Targum's phrasing, that the word of the Lord was for his help. Ellicott makes the recognition the immediate effect of the last enterprise, since the return with those ghastly spoils, and the daughter's love on top of it, forced on the king the conclusion that a higher power was at work. Gill puts the fear in its political form, that the marriage meant as an instrument of ruin looked more and more like a road to the throne, and that the designs against David would never now succeed. Keil and Delitzsch note where the enmity found its occasion to show itself in practice, namely in David's success in every engagement with the Philistines, and Ellicott's summary is that the paroxysms of jealousy had hardened into a lifelong hostility.

Why the Philistine princes chose that moment is answered two ways. Clarke and Wesley put it down to revenge, provoked by their earlier losses and by the recent killing of two hundred of their men, and Clarke adds that nothing else is known of this war except that David proved more skilful in it than any other officer the king had. Gill and Ellicott both report a rabbinic explanation instead, that the enemy had heard of the marriage and counted on the Hebrew law which exempted a newly married man from war for a year. Gill alone goes on to answer it: David understood that law better than they did, since it applied to the war commanded against the seven nations and not to a voluntary one, and even there some hold that it left the man free to go if he chose. The chapter's last clause they all take at face value, that he behaved himself more wisely than all the king's servants, and that this is why his name was so much set by.
